youtube.baslik: Case: Spinning When Getting Out of Bed (BPPV) | Lesson 292 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In a fictional adult case we evaluate posterior canal BPPV: the history and red flags, the latent, upbeating and torsional nystagmus on the Dix-Hallpike test, identifying the affected side and canal, the Epley maneuver, and reassessment after the maneuver.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Bhattacharyya et al., Clinical Practice Guideline: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (Update), Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, 2017; Barany Society, Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo: Diagnostic Criteria (2015); Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Dix-Hallpike, affected side, after the maneuver
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we evaluate, step by step, an adult who gets dizzy when getting out of bed and turning over in bed.
We will cover the history, the Dix-Hallpike finding, identifying the affected canal and side, and reassessment after the maneuver.

maddeler.metin: Spinning when turning right in bed
Each attack under half a minute

cumleler: Our case is entirely fictional: a sixty-four-year-old woman comes in with attacks of dizziness over the past five days.
She says the room spins violently when she gets out of bed in the morning, and especially when she turns to the right in bed.
Each attack lasts less than half a minute; between attacks there is only mild unsteadiness and some nausea.
A similar attack happened when she tipped her head back to reach something on a high shelf.
She has no change in hearing, no tinnitus, headache or double vision, and no difficulty speaking or swallowing.
With its brief attacks triggered by head position, this history suggests benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV.
Before positional testing, signs suggesting a central cause are asked about: double vision, and speech or swallowing problems.
Numbness and weakness in the face, arm or leg are also asked about.
A sudden, severe headache or neck pain is an important warning sign.
Dizziness that continues with the head still, and inability to stand, suggest the picture is not BPPV.
If any of these signs is present, testing is not done; the person is referred for urgent physician evaluation.
In BPPV, otoconia, or calcium carbonate crystals, break loose from the utricle and enter a semicircular canal.
The canal most easily reached in the direction of gravity is the posterior canal, so it is the one most often involved.
When the head reaches a certain position, the crystals slide within the canal and drag the fluid along.
The fluid flow deflects the cupula, which produces a brief but intense spinning sensation and nystagmus.
When the crystals stop, the flow and the symptoms stop too; this is why the attacks are short.
Sitting up, she is checked with video goggles: there is no spontaneous nystagmus and no gaze-evoked nystagmus.
Neck pain, neck or back surgery and limited movement are asked about; there is no contraindication.
Video goggles remove visual fixation, so the torsional component in particular is much easier to see.
She is told she may feel brief spinning, that she is supported against falling, and that she should keep her eyes open.
The audiogram shows an age-appropriate, symmetric, mild high-frequency loss in both ears; there is no new one-sided loss.
The posterior canal lies in a plane tilted about forty five degrees from the midline of the head.
The right posterior canal lies in the same plane as the left anterior canal; this is called the LARP plane.
With the head turned forty five degrees to the right, the right posterior canal plane aligns with the body's front-to-back plane.
When the patient is laid back in this position, the canal turns fully in the direction of gravity and the crystals move.
In the Dix-Hallpike test, the posterior canal of the lower ear is tested.
The patient sits on the examination table with legs extended.
The head is turned forty five degrees to the right.
The patient is quickly laid back; the head is supported about twenty degrees below the edge of the table.
The eyes are watched and recorded for at least thirty seconds, or until the response ends if nystagmus appears.
Then the patient is slowly brought back to sitting, and the eyes are watched again.
Nystagmus does not start as soon as she reaches the right Dix-Hallpike position.
It appears after a delay of about three seconds, called the latency.
The fast phase beats upward, toward the forehead; in the torsional part, the upper pole of the eye beats toward the lower, right ear.
The nystagmus first builds, then fades, and dies out in about twenty seconds; she feels spinning for the same time.
On the graph, we see this course as the change in slow phase velocity over time.
When she sits up, a brief, weaker nystagmus is seen in the opposite direction.
Latency, short duration and a course that first builds and then fades are typical of posterior canal canalithiasis.
The right Dix-Hallpike shows a typical response with vertigo.
The left Dix-Hallpike, done after a sufficient break, shows no nystagmus.
The supine roll test, which assesses the lateral canals, shows no horizontal nystagmus.
The findings are consistent with right posterior canal BPPV of the canalithiasis type; the diagnosis is made by the physician.
Tests should not be repeated back to back too quickly; with fatigue, the response may disappear on the second test.

sahneler.metin: Confirm brief torsional nystagmus with video recording. If the response is not typical, do not do a maneuver; refer to a physician.
cumleler: A clinical tip: the direction of brief torsional nystagmus is much clearer on a recording; record the test on video if possible.
The recording strengthens the decision about which side is involved and later comparisons.
If the nystagmus has no latency, does not fatigue, or is pure downbeating, the picture does not fit typical BPPV.
In that case no maneuver is done; the findings are recorded and the patient is referred for physician evaluation.
A canalith repositioning procedure aims to move the crystals out of the canal and back into the utricle.
The first step of the Epley maneuver is the right Dix-Hallpike position; you wait until nystagmus and spinning pass.
Then, keeping the head extended, it is slowly turned ninety degrees to the left.
Next the patient rolls onto the left side, and the head is turned another ninety degrees so the face points to the floor.
Finally the patient is slowly brought to sitting; in each position, you wait until the nystagmus stops.
Who performs the maneuver varies by country; it is done in suitable patients by an authorized, trained clinician.
The eyes are still watched with video goggles during the maneuver; in our case, brief nystagmus is also seen in the second position.
Nystagmus in the same direction as in the first position has been reported as a sign that the crystals are moving the right way.
Nystagmus in the opposite direction may suggest the crystals are sliding back toward the ampulla.
If the type of nystagmus changes, the crystals may have entered another canal; this is canal conversion, and the new canal is identified.
Throughout the maneuver, the patient is supported against falling and asked about nausea.
After a short break, the right Dix-Hallpike is repeated; there is no nystagmus or vertigo, and the result is recorded.

cumleler.yazi: The 2017 guideline of the American Academy of Otolaryngology does not advise routine postural restrictions after a posterior canal maneuver.
cumleler.ses: The twenty seventeen guideline of the American Academy of Otolaryngology does not advise routine postural restrictions after a posterior canal maneuver.

cumleler: She is told that even after a successful maneuver, mild unsteadiness may remain for a few days to a few weeks.
The guideline recommends reassessing the patient within about a month after initial treatment.
She is also told that BPPV can recur and that she can come back if a new attack happens.
If complaints persist at the one-month check, positional tests are first repeated, and the side and canal are reviewed.
If the nystagmus type has changed, another canal may be involved, and the matching maneuver is chosen.
If the picture is atypical or there is no response to repeated maneuvers, the patient is referred to a physician to look for central causes.
If unsteadiness persists after the positional nystagmus resolves, vestibular rehabilitation may help.
In older patients, fall risk is assessed and home safety measures are discussed.
Example report language: no spontaneous or gaze nystagmus was found with video goggles.
Right Dix-Hallpike showed upbeating, torsional nystagmus with about three seconds latency, lasting about twenty seconds, with vertigo.
Left Dix-Hallpike and supine roll showed no nystagmus; findings are consistent with right posterior canal BPPV.
A right Epley maneuver was done; repeat right Dix-Hallpike showed no nystagmus.
Reassessment within about a month is recommended; she was asked to return sooner if symptoms change.

maddeler.metin: Retest after the maneuver, follow up

cumleler: Attacks lasting seconds when turning in bed or getting up suggest posterior canal BPPV; red flags are asked about first.
On Dix-Hallpike, upbeating, torsional nystagmus with a few seconds of latency, lasting under a minute, is the typical finding.
In the test with the typical response, the lower ear is the affected side; the torsion also beats toward this ear.
After the maneuver, the test is repeated, routine restrictions are not advised, and reassessment follows within about a month.

sahneler.soru: Left Dix-Hallpike shows a typical response. Which canal?
sahneler.aciklama: Dix-Hallpike tests the posterior canal of _the lower ear_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: left Dix-Hallpike shows latent, upbeating, torsional nystagmus. Which canal is suspected?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the left posterior canal.
This test assesses the posterior canal of the lower ear; upbeating torsional nystagmus points to the posterior canal.
